question: Mechanical Properties of Fluids: Define pressure and write its SI unit.
gold_answer:
# Introduction

---

## Definition

Fluid pressure is defined as the normal compressive force exerted by a fluid per unit surface area of a container or object. 

Pressure acts perpendicular to the surface at every point, distributing uniformly across a level horizontal plane within a static fluid column.

---

## Characteristics

* **Isotropic Distribution:** At any given depth within a continuous static fluid body, pressure acts with equal intensity in all directions.
* **Scalar Nature:** Pressure is a scalar parameter because the force it produces acts in whatever direction face the surface points.

---

## Formula

The mechanical definition of surface pressure:

$$P = \frac{F}{A}$$

Where:
* $P$ represents the fluid pressure
* $F$ represents the normal force component acting perpendicular to the surface
* $A$ represents the total boundary area of the surface interface

---

## Metric System Units

The standard SI unit of pressure is the **Pascal ($\text{Pas}$)**, which is equivalent to a force of $1 \text{ Newton}$ acting uniformly over a surface area of $1 \text{ square meter}$.

$$1 \text{ Pa} = 1 \text{ N}/\text{m}^2 = 1 \text{ kg}/(\text{m}\cdot\text{s}^2)$$

---

## Summary

Pressure measures force distribution across a surface area, acting isotropically within fluid systems and measured internationally in Pascals.

# Pressure — Interactive Concept Card

---

## Quick Definition

**Pressure** is defined as the **force acting perpendicularly on a unit area** of a surface.

It measures how concentrated a force is over a given area.

---

## Formula Card

$$P = \frac{F}{A}$$

| Symbol | Quantity | Unit |
|--------|----------|------|
| $P$ | Pressure | Pascal (Pa) |
| $F$ | Normal Force | Newton (N) |
| $A$ | Area | m² |

---

## SI Unit

$$1 \ \text{Pascal} = 1 \ \frac{\text{N}}{\text{m}^2}$$

> **Named after:** Blaise Pascal (French mathematician & physicist)
>
> **Symbol:** Pa

---

## Key Characteristics

**① Scalar Quantity**
Pressure has magnitude only — no direction.

**② Force must be perpendicular**
Only the component of force *normal* to the surface contributes to pressure.

**③ Area inversely affects pressure**
Smaller area → Greater pressure (for same force)

---

## Intuitive Example

| Situation | Force | Area | Pressure |
|-----------|-------|------|----------|
| Nail tip | Same | Very small | **Very high** |
| Flat head | Same | Large | **Low** |

> This is why a sharp nail pierces wood easily — same force, tiny area = enormous pressure.

---

## Other Common Units

| Unit | Relation to Pa |
|------|---------------|
| **Bar** | $1 \ \text{bar} = 10^5 \ \text{Pa}$ |
| **Atmosphere (atm)** | $1 \ \text{atm} = 1.013 \times 10^5 \ \text{Pa}$ |
| **mm of Hg (Torr)** | $1 \ \text{atm} = 760 \ \text{mm Hg}$ |

---

## 💡 Important Note

> Pressure is a **scalar**, but the *force causing it* is a vector.
> In fluids, pressure acts **equally in all directions** at a point — this is **Pascal's Law**.

---

## Quick Recall

| Property | Value |
|----------|-------|
| Formula | $P = F/A$ |
| SI Unit | Pascal (Pa) |
| Dimensions | $[\text{ML}^{-1}\text{T}^{-2}]$ |
| Type | Scalar |
